title: Representing algorithms
explanation: Algorithms can be represented as flowcharts (boxes and arrows showing the flow of steps and decisions) or as pseudocode (structured English that reads like code but isn't tied to a specific language). Both let you plan logic before writing real code.

title: Linear search
explanation: Linear search checks each item in a list one at a time, from the start, until it finds the target or reaches the end. It works on unsorted lists but is slow for large lists: worst case is O(n).

title: Binary search
explanation: Binary search repeatedly halves a SORTED list, comparing the middle item to the target and discarding the half that can't contain it. Much faster than linear search on large lists: O(log n).

title: Bubble sort
explanation: Bubble sort repeatedly steps through the list, swapping adjacent items that are in the wrong order. Each pass 'bubbles' the next-largest value into place. Simple but slow: O(n squared).

title: Merge sort
explanation: Merge sort is a divide-and-conquer algorithm: split the list in half repeatedly until each part has one item, then merge the parts back together in sorted order. Much faster than bubble sort on large lists: O(n log n).
code:
def merge_sort(items):
    if len(items) <= 1:
        return items
    mid = len(items) // 2
    left = merge_sort(items[:mid])
    right = merge_sort(items[mid:])
    merged = []
    i = j = 0
    while i < len(left) and j < len(right):
        if left[i] <= right[j]:
            merged.append(left[i]); i += 1
        else:
            merged.append(right[j]); j += 1
    merged.extend(left[i:])
    merged.extend(right[j:])
    return merged

print(merge_sort([5, 1, 4, 2, 8]))  # [1, 2, 4, 5, 8]

title: Sequence, selection, iteration
explanation: The three basic building blocks of any program: sequence runs statements in order, selection (if/elif/else) chooses between branches, and iteration (for/while) repeats statements.

title: Lists (1D and 2D data structures)
explanation: A list stores an ordered collection of values, indexed from 0. A 2D list (a list of lists) is often used to represent a grid, such as a game board or table of data.
code:
grid = [[0, 0, 0], [0, 1, 0], [0, 0, 0]]
print(grid[1][1])  # 1

scores = [55, 72, 90]
scores.append(64)
print(sum(scores) / len(scores))

title: String manipulation
explanation: Strings support slicing, concatenation, and built-in methods for common tasks like changing case, searching, and splitting on a separator.
code:
name = "Computer Science"
print(name.upper())
print(name.lower())
print(name[0:8])
print(len(name))
print(name.split(" "))

title: Subroutines: functions and procedures
explanation: A subroutine is a named, reusable block of code. A function returns a value; a procedure (in pseudocode terms) performs an action without necessarily returning one. Parameters let you pass data in.

title: File handling
explanation: Programs can read from and write to text files to store data between runs. Using 'with open(...)' ensures the file is closed automatically even if an error occurs.
code:
with open("scores.txt", "w") as f:
    f.write("Alex,90\n")
    f.write("Sam,72\n")

with open("scores.txt", "r") as f:
    for line in f:
        name, score = line.strip().split(",")
        print(name, score)

title: Input validation
explanation: Validation checks that user input is sensible before it's used, e.g. checking it's a number, within a range, or not blank. It doesn't guarantee the data is correct, only that it's plausible.

title: Binary numbers
explanation: Computers store all data as binary (base 2): just 0s and 1s. An 8-bit binary number can represent 256 values (0-255). Converting binary to denary: add up the place values (128,64,32,16,8,4,2,1) where there's a 1.
code:
# Convert a denary number to an 8-bit binary string
value = 156
print(format(value, "08b"))  # 10011100

# Convert binary back to denary
print(int("10011100", 2))  # 156

title: Hexadecimal
explanation: Hexadecimal (base 16) uses digits 0-9 then A-F. It's a compact way to represent binary: each hex digit maps to exactly 4 bits, so it's often used for colour codes and memory addresses.

title: Character encoding (ASCII/Unicode)
explanation: Every character a computer displays is stored as a number. ASCII uses 7-8 bits and covers basic English characters; Unicode uses more bits and can represent characters from every written language.

title: Representing images
explanation: A bitmap image is stored as a grid of pixels. Each pixel's colour is stored as a binary value; more bits per pixel (colour depth) means more possible colours but a larger file size. Resolution is the number of pixels.

title: Data compression
explanation: Compression reduces file size. Lossless compression (e.g. run-length encoding) removes redundancy so the original can be perfectly rebuilt. Lossy compression permanently discards some data to save more space.

title: CPU architecture and the fetch-decode-execute cycle
explanation: The CPU repeatedly fetches an instruction from memory, decodes what it means, and executes it. Key components: the Control Unit (manages the cycle), the ALU (does arithmetic/logic), and registers (tiny, fast storage).

title: Factors affecting CPU performance
explanation: Clock speed (cycles per second) determines how many instructions can run per second. Cache size gives faster access to frequently used data than RAM. The number of cores lets a CPU run tasks in parallel.

title: Embedded systems
explanation: An embedded system is a computer built into a larger device to perform a specific task, e.g. a washing machine controller or a car's engine management system. Unlike a general-purpose computer, it usually runs one dedicated program.

title: Network types and topologies
explanation: A LAN (Local Area Network) covers a small area like one building; a WAN (Wide Area Network) covers a large area, e.g. connecting offices in different cities. A star topology connects every device to a central switch; a bus topology connects devices along a single cable.

title: Protocols: TCP/IP, HTTP/HTTPS
explanation: A protocol is an agreed set of rules for communication. TCP/IP breaks data into packets and routes them across networks. HTTP is used to transfer web pages; HTTPS is the encrypted version, protecting data in transit.

title: Common cyber security threats
explanation: Malware (viruses, worms, trojans) damages or spies on systems. Social engineering (phishing) tricks people into giving up information. Brute-force attacks try many passwords automatically. SQL injection inserts malicious code into a database query via an input field.
code:
-- Vulnerable if a query is built like this with untrusted input:
-- "SELECT * FROM users WHERE username = '" + input + "'"
-- Safer: use a parameterised query instead
SELECT * FROM users WHERE username = ?;

title: Relational database concepts
explanation: A relational database organises data into tables. Each table has a primary key (uniquely identifies a row) and can be linked to other tables via a foreign key, avoiding duplicated data.

title: SQL: SELECT and WHERE
explanation: SELECT retrieves data from a table; WHERE filters which rows are returned based on a condition.

title: SQL: INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE
explanation: INSERT adds a new row, UPDATE changes existing rows matching a condition, and DELETE removes rows matching a condition.

title: Ethical, legal and environmental impacts of technology
explanation: Computer science raises real-world issues: data privacy and consent (ethical/legal), the environmental cost of manufacturing and e-waste, and laws such as the Computer Misuse Act (unauthorised access) and Data Protection Act (how personal data must be handled).
